1.title: Yields Fall as the Name Becomes More Specific
1.html:
Alsace's yield rules clearly reflect the logic of "the more specific the name, the stricter the rules":

TierWhiteRed
Alsace (base, rosé 75 hl/ha)80 hl/ha60 hl/ha
Alsace + geographical denomination72 hl/ha60 hl/ha
Alsace + site name (lieu-dit)68 hl/ha60 hl/ha
Alsace Grand CruBase 55 hl/ha (PLC up to +20%, maximum 66 hl/ha)
2.title: Yield Differences by Variety (Reference Values from the Older System)
2.html:
The following are the older variety-based yield limits (the former system, shown for comparison; the current base yield limit for AOC Alsace white wine is 80 hl/ha). Even within the same tier, maximum permitted yields differed by variety — reflecting the idea that "the more refined the variety, the lower the yield needed for concentration":

100 hl/ha
Auxerrois・Chasselas・Pinot Blanc・Pinot(Klevner)・Sylvaner
90 hl/ha
Muscat・Muscat Ottonel・Riesling
80 hl/ha
Gewurztraminer・Pinot Gris
3.title: Mandatory Hand Harvesting
3.html:
In the following cases hand harvesting is mandatory and mechanical harvesting is not allowed:

  • Wines labelled with a site name (lieu-dit) where the variety is Pinot Gris or Pinot Noir
  • All Alsace Grand Cru wines
  • All wines labelled VT (Vendanges Tardives) or SGN (Sélection de Grains Nobles)

In addition, the two blended Grand Crus (Altenberg de Bergheim and Kaefferkopf) have minimum planting densities: Altenberg de Bergheim more than 5,500 vines per hectare, Kaefferkopf 4,500 vines per hectare — high density increases competition between vines and further limits natural yield.
4.question: Why is the Grand Cru base yield limit (55 hl/ha) clearly lower than that of the base Alsace tier (80 hl/ha)?
4.options.0: Because Grand Cru land is smaller and cannot carry that many vines
4.options.1: Low yields help the vine concentrate its resources on a limited number of bunches, raising concentration and quality, in line with Grand Cru's top-quality requirement
4.options.2: It is simply an old rule with no connection to quality
4.options.3: Because Grand Cru vines are usually younger and naturally yield less
4.explanation: As the top tier of the Alsace classification, Grand Cru ensures quality through a lower yield limit (55 hl/ha, about 70% of the base Alsace tier's 80 hl/ha): low yields let the vine concentrate its resources on fewer bunches, raising concentration and flavour complexity — a concrete expression of the classification logic "more specific, stricter and better".
5.keyPoints.0: Yield limits fall as the name becomes more specific: base Alsace 80 hl/ha → + denomination 72 hl/ha → + site name 68 hl/ha → Grand Cru 55 hl/ha
5.keyPoints.1: In the older system, within the same tier "noble" varieties (Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris at 80 hl/ha) had lower yield limits than volume varieties (Sylvaner etc. at 100 hl/ha)
5.keyPoints.2: Pinot Gris / Pinot Noir with a site name, all Grand Cru, and all VT / SGN must be hand-harvested
5.keyPoints.3: The two blended Grand Crus have extra minimum planting densities: Altenberg de Bergheim 5,500 vines/ha, Kaefferkopf 4,500 vines/ha
